topic: Agent CodeMode: Let Coding-Agent Scripts Call Your MCP Servers

key_points: Original 'Code Mode' post (Kenton Varda / Sunil Pai, Sept 2025) — the source of the phrase and the thesis: 'LLMs are better at writing code to call MCP than at calling MCP directly.'
Client-side Code Mode converts an MCP server's schema into a TypeScript API with doc comments instead of exposing raw JSON tool schemas; the model writes against typed function signatures.

Names the cost problem precisely: in the classic loop every intermediate result must flow back into the model's context before the next decision, so a 5-step chain pays 5 inference passes and drags 4 payloads it never reads.
Implementation runs in a Dynamic Worker / V8 isolate — no filesystem, no env vars, outbound fetch disabled by default.
Tradeoff they admit: client-side code mode requires the agent to ship with secure sandbox access.
Feb 2026 follow-up: server-side Code Mode for the entire Cloudflare API behind exactly two tools, search() and execute().

Fixed token footprint: ~1,000 tokens regardless of how many API endpoints exist; they claim 99.9% reduction (an equivalent native MCP server would be 1.17M input tokens — more than the whole context window of frontier models).
search() runs generated JS against the in-sandbox OpenAPI spec and returns only the matching endpoints; the full spec never enters model context.
execute() gets a cloudflare.request() client inside the isolate; the agent chains calls, paginates, and returns only the final object in a single execution.

Explicitly frames the design space: client-side code mode (Goose, Anthropic PTC), CLI-based discovery (MCPorter), dynamic tool search (Claude Code) — and argues server-side code mode is the only one that needs no client-side changes.
Anthropic's 'Code execution with MCP' (Nov 4 2025) — the vendor-side statement of the same pattern, and the citation everyone else links.
Presents MCP tools as a filesystem of TypeScript modules: the agent reads a tool's .ts file only when it needs that tool, instead of loading every definition upfront.
Names the two cost sources: tool definitions overload the context window, and intermediate tool results consume additional tokens (the same 2-hour meeting transcript flows through context twice).
Hard number: 150,000 tokens reduced to 2,000 tokens — a 98.7% time and cost saving.
Their sibling API feature is Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC); Anthropic also explored the pattern in 'Code Execution with MCP'.

The narrow but decisive differentiator: it reads the OAuth token your coding agent already minted (Claude Code's macOS Keychain entry 'Claude Code-credentials' / ~/.claude/.credentials.json) and speaks JSON-RPC to the MCP server directly — no API keys, no OAuth flow, no vault, no model in the loop.
Ships a Claude Code skill at .claude/skills/agent-codemode/SKILL.md — the skill is what actually makes the agent write one script instead of N tool calls.
CLI surface: agent-codemode servers / tools <server> / call <server> <tool> --arg k=v --text / types --all.
types --all emits typed TypeScript modules that self-register by merging into the McpServers interface, so a wrong key or type is a compile error with no cast at the call site.
Also reads Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, and Gemini CLI MCP configs (stdio + API-key servers); OAuth inheritance is Claude-only today.

Its own comparison table against Anthropic PTC, Cloudflare Code Mode, TanStack AI and MCPorter: credentials row is the only genuinely new thing — 'your agent's, inherited' vs everyone else's API key or private vault.

Verified-working matrix: remote HTTP MCP over OAuth, self-hosted remote MCP, plugin MCP (plugin:slack:slack), API-key HTTP/SSE, stdio subprocess. claude.ai connectors explicitly NOT supported (would require impersonating Claude Code).

Linux note that matters for a how-to: macOS is fully supported; on Linux/Windows the config-based (stdio, API-key) servers work as-is and Claude's OAuth tokens are read from ~/.claude/.credentials.json — the Keychain path is skipped.
The most-starred general library for the pattern (1,577 stars, MPL-2.0, actively updated) — 'first library for tool calls via code execution'.
Three-line API: create a CodeModeUtcpClient, register a manual/server, callToolChain('/* TypeScript */').
Publishes an independent Python benchmark study claiming $9,536/year savings at 1,000 scenarios/day, with 67% / 75% / 88% speedups for simple (2-3 tools), medium (4-7), and complex (8+) workflows.
Offers progressive tool discovery — searchTools('github pull request') returns a handful of relevant tools instead of 500 definitions.
Production measurement, not a vendor claim: 26 calls (workflow_list + schedule_list + 24 per-workflow workflow_listRuns) collapsed into 1 script.
Measured: 25,811 characters reach the agent's context on the script path vs ~3.26M on the modeled raw-tool-call path — reported as a 99.2% cost reduction.

Notable because the first version of the post was machine-drafted, got hammered on Hacker News, and was rewritten with honest measured-vs-modeled labels — useful for a 'how to measure this yourself' section.
Their standing rubric is the reusable takeaway: past roughly ten items, or any bulk fan-out, write a script instead of N tool calls.

The adversarial counterweight every how-to needs: Check Point found five memory-corruption bugs in workerd, the runtime under both Code Mode sandboxes and Cloudflare Workers; two rated Critical by Cloudflare.

Two end-to-end attacks: a cross-tenant heap swipe (out-of-bounds read in URLPattern reaching another tenant's secrets) and a Code Mode sandbox escape starting from a prompt injection (use-after-free in node:zlib) running native code on the host.
Fix guidance: managed Workers was patched; self-hosted workerd / Code Mode deployments should update to v1.20260619.1. PoC released at Black Hat USA 2026.
Takeaway for scripts-call-MCP: the sandbox is the security boundary, and code mode moves the trust boundary from 'the model picks a tool' to 'the model writes code you execute'.

The contrarian view to include for balance: 'you don't need code mode' — Dynamic Toolsets get up to 160x token reduction with 100% task success, ~96% input and ~90% total token reduction, without executing model-written code.
Their critique of pure semantic search: with no visibility into what exists, the LLM sometimes never searches at all ('how many deals do we have?' doesn't obviously imply a HubSpot deal tool).
So the honest boundary: dynamic/progressive tool discovery competes with code mode on token count while keeping the no-code-execution safety property.

The 'move the interface down a layer' argument: frontier models already have a battle-tested interface (code), so stop teaching a new JSON schema per action and expose a small set of typed capabilities in an execution environment.
Roughly 88% less context for a representative 3-service parallel workflow (CRM + support tickets + warehouse query composed with Promise.all, then filtered before it ever reaches context).
Security framing worth copying: enforce security below the model instead of wrapping every action in another bespoke tool call.

stats.fact: 40 sequential MCP tool calls collapse into 1 script: 262,159 chars (~65,500 tokens) into the model becomes 903 chars (~226 tokens) — 290x less, 99.66% saved, measured on a live workspace of 39 Linear tickets.
In a tool-call loop those 262,159 characters are re-read on every subsequent turn, while the script pays once — so the measured ratio is described as a floor, not a ceiling.

Cloudflare's server-side Code Mode covers ~2,500 API endpoints at a fixed ~1,000 tokens; the equivalent native MCP server (full schemas) is 1,170,523 tokens and even the minimal-schema version is 244,047 tokens.
Anthropic measures code execution with MCP at 150,000 tokens down to 2,000 tokens — a 98.7% cost and time saving.
Independent Python benchmark: $9,536/year saved at 1,000 scenarios/day, with 67% / 75% / 88% faster runs for 2-3, 4-7, and 8+ tool workflows.
Production job: 26 tool calls (1 workflow_list + 1 schedule_list + 24 workflow_listRuns) → 1 script; 25,811 chars reach context vs ~3.26M on the raw tool-call path (99.2% reduction).
Code Mode adds 10-50ms of compile + isolate startup per turn and shifts the primary failure mode from 'model picked the wrong tool' to 'generated code threw at runtime'.

On a 49-tool server, classic MCP spends ~29,400 tokens per turn on tool descriptions (294,000 tokens across a 10-turn conversation ≈ $0.44 at ~$15/M Opus input) vs a one-time ~1,000-token type-surface load for code mode.

agent-codemode: npm package 0.1.1, MIT, zero runtime dependencies, engines node>=18, ~30 GitHub stars, ~31 npm downloads in the last month. The repo has no npm-org or vendor backing — it is a single-maintainer tool.
By contrast @utcp/code-mode (the general library) saw 5,637 npm downloads in the last month, and cloudflare/mcp has 903 stars — the ecosystem around the pattern is far bigger than any one CLI.

Check Point Research found 5 memory-corruption bugs in workerd (2 Critical), including a Code Mode sandbox escape reachable from prompt injection; self-hosted Code Mode should update to workerd v1.20260619.1.
Speakeasy's counter-datapoint: Dynamic Toolsets reach up to 160x token reduction with ~96% input / ~90% total reduction and 100% task success — without executing model-written code.

Adoption signal from Hacker News: 'Code Mode: the better way to use MCP' (84 points, Sept 2025), jx-codes/codemode-mcp Show HN (87 points), 'Open Source and Local Code Mode MCP in Deno Sandboxes' (76 points), and the 99.2% cost-reduction post (62 points, 69 comments) — the pattern has sustained discussion across a year, not a single launch spike.

angles: The one-line thesis, then proof: LLMs write code better than they orchestrate tool calls — and the reason is training data. Models have seen billions of lines of TypeScript/JavaScript and only synthetic, contrived JSON tool-call blobs. Code mode stops fighting that asymmetry.

The last-mile insight nobody else ships: your coding agent already completed the OAuth dance for every MCP server you use. That token is sitting on disk, reachable only by a model deciding to make one tool call at a time. agent-codemode reads the token the agent already minted, so the setup cost is literally zero — no .env, no vault, no separate `auth` step (the row where MCPorter, Cloudflare, Anthropic PTC and TanStack AI all require credentials).

Name the two cost sources separately, because they have different fixes: (1) tool definitions loaded upfront — fixed by typed clients / progressive discovery; (2) intermediate results round-tripping through context — fixed by running the loop inside code. Most blog posts blur these; separating them is the article's spine.

The round-trip column is the one you feel. Tokens are the number in the invoice; wall-clock is the number the human notices. 40 sequential calls each stall on a model deciding what to ask next — a script makes the same 40 requests back-to-back.

Determinism is an underrated selling point: counting occurrences across 262,159 characters by reading them is something a model does approximately (and can get wrong while still having spent 65,500 tokens). Code gets it exactly right.

The script outlives the session — and this kills the obvious objection that code mode on top of MCP on top of code mode is a useless extra layer. It isn't a layer; it's the model leaving. A job that moves three tickets doesn't need reasoning, only the token, and the token is already there. Cron/CI gate with no model and no tokens.

Honest limits section: the claude.ai connector path is out of scope by design (would require impersonating Claude Code), OAuth inheritance is Claude-only for now, and on Linux/Windows only the config-based (stdio, API-key) servers work as-is. Say this rather than discovering it live.

Security is now the real cost of code mode: executing model-authored code moves the trust boundary. Cite the workerd sandbox escape (prompt injection → use-after-free in node:zlib → native code on the host) and give the concrete mitigation — run in a sandbox with no ambient network egress and no env vars, and pass tools, not credentials, into the execution context.

Give the honest threshold for when NOT to use it: classic tool calling is still correct under ~3-4 chained calls, for <10 tools, and when your client is Claude Desktop/Cursor/VS Code on classic MCP. Speakeasy's Dynamic Toolset result (160x, no code execution) is the credible non-code-mode alternative and deserves a fair row in the comparison table.

The 'is this just a fad?' counter is strong: Hacker News discussion spans Sept 2025 → Aug 2026 with independent implementations from Deno sandboxes, UTCP, Check Point's security research, Stainless's SDK code mode, and production numbers from Agent Swarm. Three independent stacks arriving at the same architecture within a couple of quarters is what turns a trick into substrate.
